newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chanel goes Nordic, Lacroix stays with splendour.
newsitem.headline: Chanel goes Nordic, Lacroix stays with splendour.

text.p: German designer Karl Lagerfeld's haute couture designs for Chanel took on the stark dream-like aura of an Ingmar Bergman film on the final day of the Autumn-Winter fashion season.
Pale women with long Raphaelite waves clad in smoky chiffon gowns, their empire bodices paved with crusty pearls and crystals, seemed to have stepped from a Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale.

Severe black coats hugging narrow, angular shoulders and buttoned high up on the neck like a priest's cassock, alongside wool suits with A-line skirts covering the knee -- gave the collection a dowdiness that rang false, as if Lagerfeld had moved into terrain unfamiliar to him. There was also an almost puritanical absence of accessories and jewelery.
A tree stretched its branches across a dress of organza the colour of a northern sky and chandelier crystals spilled from the narrow sleeves of a powder blue satin gown.
But suddenly, there came a grotesque coat of rasta wool, huge stoles and trains of ragged feathers and and tattered tulle, and new British model Karen Elson as a macabre bride in gobs of black veil.
There was an almost audible sigh of relief when a second bride emerged -- Lagerfeld's new muse, Dutch model Esther -- resembling a princess from The Wild Swans draped in misty organza.
"I though it was beautiful, inventive and full of modern clothes that real women can wear. It was one of the highlights of the Paris season," said Dawn Mello, president of Bergdorf Goodman said.

Lagerfeld, who hails from northern Germany, said his collection was flavoured by the music of composers like the Norwegian Edvard Grieg and Finland's Jean Sibelius, and the works of playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen.
"My inspiration came from my origins, literature, music, Grieg, Sibelius and everything important that has come out of the north, where my father was born."

French designer Christian Lacroix came from the other side of the spectrum, showing the steamy side of his native Mediterranean in Spanish lace veils, gold arabesques on a coral brocade military jacket and persimmon satin for gowns modeled after the santons -- little clay figures -- of Naples.

A true believer in the artisanry that makes haute couture impossible to reproduced en masse, Lacroix's taste for splendour knows no limits -- a patchwork sheath with lace and sequin bodice came with quilted violet jacket, while a gown of iridescent taffeta changed from copper to turquoise in the light, its corseted damask bustier stamped with gold leaves.
Sending out two bridal gowns instead of the traditional one seemed to be the thing to do this season.
Lacroix dressed one in black tulle streaked with silver sequins, and another in coral satin with roses in her hair.

Asked by a reporter if he wasn't overdoing it, Lacroix replied: "We need lots of wedding gowns because its the principal industry of haute couture. One often hears people say that haute couture is never seen in the street. But it is seen at weddngs. Bridal gowns are our most important orders."
Lacroix said his generous use of red and black were inspired by his interest in bullfighting.
"I was born under the sign of Taurus and I'm an aficionado. Red and black are the most beautiful, vibrant and sensual colours for me, and the most energetic," he said.
American actress Demi Moore, a guest at several shows this week described the collection as "wonderful, spectacular".
Asked whether she could see herself in any of the clothes, Moore answered hesitantly: "I think there are quite a few pieces that were very wearable."
